title: Al-Buruj: the constellations
hook: the people of the ditch who were burned for their faith (85:4–8)

segments.voice: Yesterday: At-Tariq, the night visitor, the piercing star. Your line was every soul has a guardian.

Dubai's skyline has a needle in the middle of it: the Burj Khalifa. Burj means tower. In the plural, buruj, it's the name of the surah before At-Tariq, and there it means the great towers of the night sky: the constellations, the mansions of the stars. The surah opens looking up. But it quickly looks down, into a trench in the ground, at a scene that is hard to hear: people burned for what they believed, while others sat and watched.
screen: `BURJ — A TOWER.` → `BURUJ — THE TOWERS OF THE SKY.` → `A TRENCH IN THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: Surah eighty-five swears by the sky with its constellations, by the promised Day, and by the witness and what is witnessed. Then verse four: destroyed were the people of the ditch, al-ukhdud, the fire full of fuel, as they sat around it, witnessing what they were doing to the believers. Verse eight gives the only charge against the victims: they had nothing against them except that they believed in God, the Mighty, the Praised. The Qur'an doesn't name who they were. The commentators offer two main accounts. One is a long hadith in Muslim's collection about a boy, a king and a monk: the boy's faith spreads to a whole town, and the king has trenches dug and fires lit for anyone who won't turn back. The other, told by Ibn Ishaq and the commentators, connects it to Najran, in southern Arabia, where a king named Dhu Nuwas is reported to have killed the Christians of the town who would not give up their faith. In that reading, the believers the Qur'an honors here were Christians. Either way, the surah doesn't glorify the fire, or ask anyone to seek it. It condemns the people who lit it, and it sees the ones who stood firm. Verse ten leaves a door open: those who persecuted believers, and then did not repent, face the punishment. And then did not repent. Even there, the way back isn't shut. People of many faiths, and none, have been punished for belief, and still are. The surah keeps them in view.
screen: `THE SKY, THE DAY, THE WITNESS.` · `AL-UKHDUD — THE PEOPLE OF THE DITCH.` · `THE BOY AND THE KING, OR NAJRAN.` · `AND THEN DID NOT REPENT.` · then, large: `FAITH UNDER FIRE.`

segments.voice: Hold in mind people who are suffering for their beliefs right now, somewhere in the world; no names needed, just a family, a place of worship, a person in a cell. Hold them steadily, the way the surah does, without looking away. If you pray, you can ask for them in your own words.
Al-Buruj. The constellations, the towers of the sky, and the name of Surah eighty-five, which remembers the people of the ditch. Today's word.
Your line: faith under fire. Their only charge was that they believed. Day two hundred four.

howItsDone: Muslims remember the people of the ditch as believers who held firm under persecution; the hadith of the boy and the king is a well-known story told to children and in sermons about steadfastness.

original.note: Arabic: the ditch or trench, from kh-d-d, a furrow cut in the ground (Qur'an 85:4).

trapdoor: what you thought: a surah about the stars.
what it means: under the constellations, a scene of believers burned for their faith, and a verdict on those who watched.
what a scholar hears: burj also gives the modern word for a tower; Sahih Muslim 3005 tells the boy and the king; Ibn Ishaq's Sira gives the Najran account of Dhu Nuwas.

chat.says: Who were the people of the ditch in Surah al-Buruj?
options: Believers burned for their faith; the surah condemns those who lit the fire.
Soldiers who dug a trench to defend Medina in a famous battle.
People punished for worshipping idols, as a warning to everyone.
chat.meaning: Verse eight: their only charge was that they believed in God. The Qur'an doesn't name them; commentators give two accounts.

buruj.meaning: towers; here the constellations of the night sky

al-ukhdud.meaning: the ditch, the trench of fire

Najran.meaning: a town in southern Arabia linked to one account

Dhu Nuwas.meaning: a king reported to have killed Najran's Christians

Ibn Ishaq.meaning: an early biographer of the Prophet

notes: All Qur'an text paraphrased today (not sure enough of Pickthall's exact wording of 85:1–8).
Sahih Muslim 3005 cited from memory; confirm.
Najran: Dhu Nuwas (Yusuf As'ar Yath'ar) and the massacre of Christians c. 523 CE are attested in Syriac sources and Himyarite inscriptions; confirm date and wording 'some historians find traces'.
The line 'people of many faiths, and none, have been punished for belief' is a general statement; Keeper may refine.
